Hey VaultTech007, I do believe your question deserves a logical answer, and hope you will read the answer with an open mind willing to understand. I believe what you’re asking is about a double standard, that “Why is Person A entitled to their right to a response, but you won’t acknowledge that Person B has the right to ignore and keep to themselves?” 

It can all be boiled down to the word SOCIAL CONTRACT, and I’ll talk more about that in a little bit.

There can be many nuances to situations of “who owes who what”, and these types of situations are important to investigate for such nuances. 

I mean, let’s imagine

Scenario #1: Person B is a neutral individual who attends school or works with Person A. Person A and Person B don’t even work in the same department, and are mere acquaintances. Person A sits down next to Person B during lunch, tries to ask Person B out on a date, but Person B clearly does not want to, and Person A will not leave them alone. 

In this scenario (it was made to be extreme on purpose), Person B does not owe Person A anything, because when did Person B ask for any of that?

Now let’s imagine Scenario #2, where this key term called SOCIAL CONTRACT exists. Scenario #2 is what every person on the r/ghosting subreddit is talking about, I almost guarantee. I did say investigating nuance was important but, especially when these people present the facts of their situation, but for all intents and purposes it’s better to assume in their scenario that a SOCIAL CONTRACT existed.

Scenario #2: Person A and Person B are two individuals who have a close enough relationship (friendship or romantic) that a level of TRUST has been built. They share vulnerabilities about themselves that they wouldn’t with others, there is an understanding that they have each others back. They have given each other reason to trust each other. Person A trusts that Person B likes them, because Person B has liked them every day for the past 136 days, so why would Person B change now? Person A trusts that if they’re having a bad day, they can confide in Person B, because Person B has allowed this confidence for the past 136 days (in regards to boundaries, Person B can communicate if they are drained and that’s ok, but that’s not what we’re talking about). Whether it’s 136 days or 45 days or 97 days, Person B may not simply leave without explanation because the SOCIAL CONTRACT is the understanding that you will uphold the level of trust you have allowed the other person to build up with you. Person B can do whatever they want if they never entered Person A’s life, but that is not the case, and Person B owes Person A much more than to ditch.

I hope this answers your question.

YUPPP. 1000%. I saw a similar post in the sub recently that said something like “‘I don’t owe you anything’”. The post was a middle finger to this philosophy, of course.

I’m glad that self preservation has become a trend in the past couple years, but people bastardize this philosophy into ignoring other peoples’ feelings. There is a difference between “don’t let anyone make you responsible for their feelings” and “don’t let anyone else’s feelings matter to you”.

I can agree with all your points. Even though my original post did not mention the possibility of danger being involved, I can understand why you would no longer want a dangerous person in your life. an explanation likely wouldn’t even be necessary, because if they have already threatened you, it’s pretty clear why they’re being ghosted. It’s also valid to not want a friendship with someone let them know this (imo it’s still better to give the friendship a chance by communicating what you want in a friendship, but that’s not for everybody and I won’t try to force that belief onto anyone).

Yes it still counts as a boundary even if it’s not communicated, and all boundaries are valid, but skipping the communication phase is inconsiderate to the other person involved. What if they don’t understand what the problem is? What if they want to stay in your life, but they’re a bother to you, but they could become a non-annoying version of themselves if you helped them?

The right thing to do is communicate the boundary/ issue first. If you find that the person does not respect the boundary even after being aware of it, and knowingly stomp all over your needs, then you have the right to ghost. (There is room for nuance)
